'''Donald Paul Merrifield''' {{post-nominals|list=[[Society of Jesus|SJ]]}} (November 14, 1928 – February 25, 2010) was an American [[Jesuit]] who served as the 11th president of Loyola University of Los Angeles.  He became the first president of Loyola Marymount University president upon Loyola University's merger with Marymount College in 1973 and remained as the school's president until 1984.<ref name=latimes>{{cite news|first=Keith|last=Thursby|title=Donald P. Merrifield dies at 81; former president of Loyola Marymount |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-donald-merrifield2-2010mar02-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=2010-03-03 |access-date=2010-03-10}}</ref> Under Merrifield, Loyola Marymount went through a period of rapid expansion in which thirteen new buildings were constructed on the main campus.<ref name=lmu/>

==Biography==
===Early life===
Merrifield was born in [[Los Angeles]] on November 14, 1928.<ref name=latimes/> He graduated from [[Inglewood High School (California)|Inglewood High School]]. He received his [[bachelor's degree]] in [[physics]] from [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1950.<ref name=latimes/> He went on to obtain a [[master's degree]] in physics from [[University of Notre Dame]] in 1951 and his [[doctorate]] in physics from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (M.I.T.) in 1962.<ref name=latimes/>

===Career===
Donald Merrifield entered the [[Society of Jesus]] in 1951 and was [[Ordained#Eastern.2C Roman.2C and Anglican Christianity|ordained]] a [[Roman Catholic]] priest in 1965 at [[Blessed Sacrament Catholic Church, Hollywood]].<ref name=hch>{{cite news|title=Past Loyola Marymount head Father Donald Merrifield fed Ala Moana Park's homeless|url=http://www.hawaiicatholicherald.com/Home/tabid/256/newsid884/2920/Default.aspx|work=[[Hawaii Catholic Herald]]|date=2010-03-04|access-date=2010-03-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101007125658/http://hawaiicatholicherald.com/Home/tabid/256/newsid884/2920/Default.aspx|archive-date=2010-10-07|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He taught [[physics]] at the [[University of San Francisco]], [[Santa Clara University]]<ref name=hch/> and Loyola University of Los Angeles before becoming president of Loyola in 1969. He also worked as a [[consultant]] at [[NASA]]'s [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] in [[Pasadena, California]] from 1962 until 1969.<ref name=latimes/><ref name=lmu/>

===Loyola Marymount University===
Merrifield was appointed as the 11th President of the Loyola University of Los Angeles in 1969. Instead of elaborate inauguration celebrations, he asked that celebrations be kept simple so extra funds could be spent on minority [[scholarships]].<ref name=latimes/> A strong advocate for [[Interfaith dialogue|interfaith]] relations, Merrifield had [[Rabbi]] [[Alfred Wolf (rabbi)|Alfred Wolf]] give the [[invocation]] at his inauguration.<ref name=lmu>{{cite news|title=Former LMU President Donald Merrifield, S.J. Dies at 81|url=http://newsroom.lmu.edu/newsroompressreleases/Former_LMU_President_Donald_Merrifield__S_J__Dies_at_81.htm|work=[[Loyola Marymount University]]|access-date=2010-03-10|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719231606/http://newsroom.lmu.edu/newsroompressreleases/Former_LMU_President_Donald_Merrifield__S_J__Dies_at_81.htm|archive-date=2011-07-19}}</ref>

When Loyola University and nearby Marymount College merged and assumed the name [[Loyola Marymount University]], Merrifield was selected to remain president of the university.<ref name=latimes/> The academic vice president of Marymount College, Sister Renee Harrangue, R.S.H.M., Ph.D., was appointed Provost. Under Fr. Merrifield, thirteen new buildings were constructed on Loyola Marymount's [[Westchester, Los Angeles, California|Westchester]] neighborhood of Los Angeles.<ref name=latimes/>

The thirteen buildings constructed during Merrifield's tenure as president include the Von der Ahe Communication Arts Building, the George Page Baseball Stadium, Doolan Hall, [[Gersten Pavilion]], Burns Fine Art Center, the Laband Art Gallery, the Leavey Faculty Center and the Loyola Apartments.<ref name=lmu/>

Merrifield also oversaw the expansion of [[Loyola Law School]]'s campus in [[Pico-Union]], near [[downtown Los Angeles]].<ref name=lmu/> Merrifield and the university commissioned internationally known [[architect]] [[Frank Gehry]] to design the new campus, which was needed to accommodate increased enrollment.<ref name=lmu/>

He also emphasized increased minority enrollment in the university's admissions process through [[scholarship]]s, recruitment drives and [[Student financial aid (United States)|financial aid]].<ref name=latimes/><ref name=lmu/> Loyola Marymount added [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latino]] and [[African American studies]] programs to its curriculum during his time in office.<ref name=lmu/> Merrifield also helped to form the Loyola Marymount Mexican American Alumni Association in 1981.<ref name=lmu/>

He worked closely with the brothers of the [[Missionaries of Charity]] to benefit the [[homeless]] of Los Angeles.<ref name=latimes/>

Merrifield stepped down as president of Loyola Marymount in 1984 and was succeeded by [[James N. Loughran]], S.J. However, he remained at the university as its [[chancellor (education)|chancellor]] until 2002.<ref name=latimes/><ref name=ha/>

===Later life===
Merrifield was assigned to the Jesuit community in [[Honolulu, Hawaii]], in 2003.<ref name=ha>{{cite news |title=Merrifield served Oahu's poor |url=http://the.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2010/Mar/09/ln/hawaii3090324.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101214073326/http://the.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2010/Mar/09/ln/hawaii3090324.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2010-12-14 |work=[[Honolulu Advertiser]] |date=2010-03-09 |access-date=2010-03-10 }}</ref> While living in Hawaii Merrifield worked with Oahu's [[Hispanic]] population, a [[prison ministry]], and the Catholic community in the [[Mānoa]]-Punahou area.<ref name=ha/> He continued to be actively involved in university and student life in Hawaii.<ref name=ha/> He served on the [[board of governors]] for [[Chaminade University of Honolulu]].<ref name=ha/> He also became involved with the [[Newman Center]] at the [[University of Hawaii at Manoa]], where he led retreats for students.<ref name=ha/>

Merrifield provided [[breakfast]] for dozens of homeless at [[Ala Moana Beach Park]] twice a week, using his own money.<ref name=ha/> The breakfasts gradually became known as "Fr. Don's Kitchen," inspiring Honolulu area parishes, namely St. Pius X and Sacred Heart, to offer breakfasts to approximately 360 homeless people at parks around the city.<ref name=ha/>

==Last years==
He moved to an [[assisted living]] facility in for elderly Jesuits in [[Los Gatos, California]] in 2008.<ref name=latimes/> Merrifield died from a [[heart attack]] at Good Samaritan Hospital in [[San Jose, California]], on February 25, 2010, at the age of 81.<ref name=ha/>
